extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: News/blog reporting on research retractions and the integrity issues that prompted them, summarizing institutional investigations and journal notices. Focused on describing why papers were retracted (e.g., image problems) and the response from institutions and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific integrity (institutional commitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: MD Anderson is committed to the highest standards of scientific integrity. Any scientific work that does not adhere to the highest standards of scientific integrity is not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should publicly affirm commitment to integrity, support journals when questions are raised, and take steps to correct the scientific record. The page quotes MD Anderson's statement as rationale for retractions and institutional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images must not be reused to represent different experimental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Images had been reused to represent different experimental conditions.” (quoted from multiple retraction notices)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reused images that ostensibly show different samples/conditions are a grounds for retraction. The article gives multiple concrete examples (e.g., actin immunoblot in Fig. 1D and JNK1 immunoblot in Fig. 5B reused; U266 nuclei image reused across papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Images must not be inappropriately manipulated
rubrics_metrics.description: “Analysis by the Journal with image analysis software determined that Fig. 4C had been inappropriately manipulated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inappropriate manipulation (beyond acceptable adjustments) detected by journals is treated seriously and can trigger retraction. The page shows a journal explicitly stating manipulation detected as the reason for retracting a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite figure assembly must be transparent and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fig. 1B was assembled from a composite of many images.” (noted in a retraction notice)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembling figures from multiple images without proper labeling or disclosure that they are composites can be considered misleading and has been cited as a reason for retraction in the examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunoblot (loading control) reuse is unacceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple retraction notices cite reuse of actin immunoblots and JNK immunoblots across different figures and panels (e.g., “the actin immunoblot in Fig. 2A was reused as the actin immunoblot in Fig. 3B”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing immunoblot images (including loading controls) to represent different experiments or panels is explicitly called out as misconduct in the notices; such reuse undermines credibility of the reported results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image flipping or mirrored reuse to masquerade as different data is prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: “The IKK immunoblot from Fig. 2G was flipped horizontally and reused as the IKK immunoblot in Fig. 2H.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering orientation (flipping) and reusing the same image to represent distinct experiments is a form of manipulation cited in retraction notices and is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals and institutions should investigate allegations and correct the record (retraction, correction, expression of concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Journal of Biological Chemistry issued retractions after an MD Anderson investigation determined image issues; the article also notes the researcher has 17 corrections (11 figure-related) and two expressions of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigations determine problems, journals/institutions should take corrective actions—retractions, corrections, or EOCs—to preserve the integrity of the literature. The page uses these actions as the mechanism by which the scientific record is corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of image analysis software as part of detection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Analysis by the Journal with image analysis software determined that Fig. 4C had been inappropriately manipulated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may employ automated or software-assisted image analysis to identify suspicious duplications/manipulations; findings from such analyses have been used as evidence in retraction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should specify the problematic items and how they were flawed
rubrics_metrics.description: Each retraction notice quoted lists the specific figures/panels and how they were misused or manipulated (e.g., which figures had reused panels, which images were flipped, cross-paper reuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice (illustrated by the examples) is for retraction notices to be explicit about which figures/panels are problematic and how, to clarify the basis for the retraction and inform readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track citation and correction history as indicators of impact and concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reports citation counts for each retracted paper (e.g., 84 citations, 64 citations) and tallies corrections and expressions of concern associated with the researcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting citation counts and correction/EOC history helps readers assess the potential impact of problematic work and the extent of record changes; high-cited retractions indicate wider potential influence of flawed research.
